quote:
Our review shows an unambiguous and con-
sistent result for the tenure variable; landowners are
more likely than tenants to adopt agroforestry and
other conservation technologies. When included, the
tenure variable is signiﬁcant in 64–72% of the cases
considered.

relationship.outcome_raw: tenure (owner vs renter) is positively associated with the probability that smallholders adopt agroforestry and other conservation technologies
relationship.direction_cue:
landowners are
more likely than tenants to adopt

context.region: tropics (32 studies; Asia, Africa, Latin America; two USA and one Canada study in the expanded sample)
context.practice_as_described: agroforestry adoption on smallholder farms: alley farming, live hedges, contour hedgerows, homegardens, tree planting, intercropping perennials, live fences and windbreaks (Table 1); expanded sample adds contour farming, bunds, grass strips and other soil and water conservation
context.note: Vote-counting meta-analysis of 32 multivariate household-survey adoption studies (partial sample: 22-23 studies of planting trees or hedgerows on farms; expanded sample adds soil and water conservation studies), mostly tropical Asia and Africa (Indonesia, Philippines, India most represented). Statistical significance only; no effect sizes (marginal probabilities not reported). Authors caution that significance-reporting bias inflates the shares. Authors' rationale (p4): tenure insecurity is long-term risk that undermines investments with a long gestation period. Re-reviewed full PDF pp1-14 on 2026-11-04 under v1.9.4. Source performs its own vote-count synthesis; primary_measured identifies that original aggregate analysis, not new household observations. Count this review once; its constituent studies are not independent replication of this review. Table 1 includes homegardens and other systems, but no family-specific inference is made: cross_family is retained, with no distribution to homegardens or any other family. Partial agroforestry sample and expanded agroforestry plus non-agroforestry conservation sample must remain distinct. Source p5 says 22 partial studies and nine remaining within 32; Table 2 footnote says 23. This internal denominator inconsistency is retained, not repaired. Reported vote percentages are neither adoption effect sizes nor calibration thresholds. No pooled marginal probability or common significance cut-off is available. Purposive selection, publication/significance bias, equal study weights and absent quality adjustment limit transfer (pp11-12). Table 2 p6 reports 11 included, six significant positive, one negative, four insignificant; Table 3 p7 reports 18 included, 12 positive, one negative, five insignificant. Thus prose p10 saying unambiguous/consistent overstates unanimity. Direction describes dominant association only, retaining contrary and null votes. Owner-versus-tenant proxy does not encompass all tenure arrangements or legal security.

attribution: Original vote-count synthesis by Pattanayak et al. (2003); constituent adoption studies listed in Table 1, native PDF p4. No new primary household data; no independent replication credit against constituent studies.

quote:
Extension and Training: Investigators typically re-
port binary variables on whether the household or
farmer has received any training in the technology
under consideration or has any access to extension
services. Such measures of ‘extension and training’
are found in 27% and 32% of the partial and ex-
panded samples. They generate the expected positive
correlation with adoption in 100% (90%) of the par-
tial (expanded) sample, when included.

relationship.outcome_raw: access to extension services or training in the technology is positively associated with the probability of agroforestry adoption

quote:
Credit/Savings: Availability of credit or savings is
included in only 5% and 6% of the partial and ex-
panded samples. This is not surprising, given that for-
mal credit is rarely available in rural areas in tropical
countries. However, when included it has the ex-
pected positive and statistically signiﬁcant inﬂuence
in 100% of the cases. It is possible that credit was in-
cluded in the analysis only when it was found to be
statistically signiﬁcant.

relationship.outcome_raw: availability of credit or savings is positively associated with the probability of agroforestry adoption

quote:
Labor: The labor variable is typically based on ei-
ther the size of the family or the number of adults
and/or males in the family. Measures of labor endow-
ments have been included in 68% and 74% of the
partial and expanded samples and are statistically sig-
niﬁcant in 33% and 39% of the models that include
them in the partial and expanded samples. The sign
of the correlation is found to be quite consistently
positive across the cases.

relationship.outcome_raw: household labour endowment (family size, number of adults or males) is positively associated with the probability of agroforestry adoption

quote:
Distance to market: Probably because of the lim-
ited by the availability of geographical detail in the
data, only 32% of our partial sample and 26% of the
expanded sample include this variable. However, dis-
tance to market is statistically signiﬁcant in over 70%
of these cases, with the expected negative correlation.
